questions.q: When should you use `pd.MultiIndex.from_product` to build a panel index rather than `set_index` on existing columns?
options: When you already know every combination of levels (e.g. every date crossed with every ticker) and want to generate the full index
Only when the DataFrame has no missing values
When you want a single-level index instead of a hierarchical one
from_product and set_index always produce different results on the same data
questions.explain: from_product is the right tool when every combination of level values is known in advance; set_index builds the same hierarchical shape but from an existing long/tidy DataFrame's real observations.

questions.q: What does `panel.xs("AAPL", level="ticker")` do differently from `panel.loc[("2025-01-02", "AAPL")]`?
options: xs selects on a named inner level across all outer values and can drop that level from the result; .loc with a full tuple selects one exact row
They are exactly equivalent in every case
xs only works on columns, never on the index
xs always raises an error if the level name doesn't match the first level
questions.explain: `.xs` performs a cross-section on a named level (here, every date for AAPL) and can drop that level from the output, while a full tuple in `.loc` pinpoints a single exact row.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `resample` and `rolling` on a time series?
options: They are interchangeable and always produce identical output
resample changes the frequency of the data via an aggregation into new buckets; rolling keeps the same frequency and computes a statistic over a trailing window
rolling can only be used on MultiIndex DataFrames
resample requires timezone-aware timestamps; rolling does not support dates at all
questions.explain: resample collapses observations into coarser time buckets (e.g. daily to weekly), producing fewer rows; rolling preserves the original frequency and row count while computing a trailing-window statistic at each point.

questions.q: What happens if you try to compare a naive pandas Timestamp with a timezone-aware one?
options: pandas silently assumes the naive timestamp is UTC
pandas raises an error rather than guessing, because the same clock time means different instants in different zones
The naive timestamp is automatically localized to the system's local timezone
Both timestamps are converted to Unix epoch seconds for comparison
questions.explain: pandas deliberately raises rather than silently guessing when comparing naive and timezone-aware timestamps, since '9:30' means a different absolute instant in New York versus London.

questions.q: Why does `friday + BusinessDay(1)` land on Monday instead of Saturday, unlike `friday + pd.Timedelta(days=1)`?
options: BusinessDay is calendar-aware and skips weekends; Timedelta just adds a fixed duration regardless of the calendar
BusinessDay always adds exactly 3 days regardless of the starting day
pd.Timedelta cannot be added to a Timestamp at all
BusinessDay(1) and Timedelta(days=1) are identical; the example is incorrect
questions.explain: DateOffset subclasses like BusinessDay understand calendar structure and skip weekends (and, with CustomBusinessDay, holidays), while Timedelta simply adds a fixed amount of elapsed time.
